title: Farmer's Almanac: Literature to Poop To
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore the history of the Old Farmer's Almanac and its rival the Farmer's Almanac. They cover the medieval origins of almanacs, satirical parody almanacs including Rabelais and Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanac, Robert Bailey Thomas founding the Farmer's Almanac in 1792/1793, the addition of "Old" in 1832 and John Jenks's cover art, the rivalry between the two almanacs, Ray Geiger's marketing campaigns, the hole punched in the corner for hanging, the Abraham Lincoln "Almanac Trial," and the accuracy of their long-range weather forecasts and how they are calculated. The episode closes with a listener email about Noam Chomsky.

segments.title: Composting outhouse and reason for the episode
segments.summary: Chuck explains he keeps an old Farmer's Almanac in the outhouse at his camp, which has a composting toilet. Josh mentions he ordered his own copy. They introduce the topic.

segments.name: Almanac history and oldest periodical claim
segments.title: Origins and age of the Old Farmer's Almanac
segments.summary: The Old Farmer's Almanac has been published since 1792 and is called the oldest continuously published periodical in North America. Josh compares it to the Hartford Courant (1764) and the Swiss Post and Domestic Times (1645).

segments.title: What almanacs contain and their medieval roots
segments.summary: Almanacs mixed farming tips, astronomical charts, moon phases, recipes, jokes, poetry, and long-range weather forecasts. The word almanac is traced to medieval French astronomers, and early almanacs were handwritten before the printing press.

segments.title: Parody almanacs and Poor Richard's Almanac
segments.summary: Rabelais produced a parody almanac in 1532, starting a satirical trend. Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard's Almanac, written under the name Richard Saunders, was popular and gave us sayings such as early to bed, early to rise.

segments.title: Robert Bailey Thomas and his education
segments.summary: Robert Bailey Thomas grew up on an educated farm family with a library. He worked as a schoolteacher and bookbinder and studied at Osgood Carlton's School of Mathematics in Boston before starting his almanac.

segments.title: First edition contents and Thomas's writing style
segments.summary: The first Farmer's Almanac appeared in 1793 as a 46-page book with astronomical calculations, farmer's calendars, and entertaining material. Thomas's witty writing, math puzzles, and a cider-making story made it popular. Each month's page header read as 'half thirty one days.' Thomas edited 53 editions before dying in 1846.

segments.title: Adding 'Old' to the name and cover art
segments.summary: Philip Michael Thomas changed the name to the Old Farmer's Almanac in 1832 to distinguish it from competitors. John Jenks later dropped the change and began the cover art in 1851. The cover design still in use today traces to Jenks.

segments.title: Farmer's Almanac rivalry and Ray Geiger's campaigns
segments.summary: The newer Farmer's Almanac, founded in 1818, has long rivaled the Old Farmer's Almanac. Janis Stillman was the first woman editor of the Old Farmer's Almanac. Ray Geiger ran the Farmer's Almanac for decades, running publicity campaigns and saving place names on US postmarks.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break for an iHeartRadio sponsor.

segments.title: Transition to almanac lore
segments.summary: Brief transition into the lore surrounding almanacs.

segments.title: Hanging hole in the corner and rival claims
segments.summary: Both almanacs claim to have started the hole in the top left corner so customers can hang them up. Both companies tell the same story and each says it was first.

segments.title: The Almanac Trial with Abraham Lincoln
segments.summary: Lincoln defended a friend of his son accused of murder. He used a farmer's almanac to show the moon was not bright at 11 pm, undermining a witness's testimony. Both almanacs claim credit, and the hosts discuss Lincoln's later moves on a different prisoner.

segments.title: Chuck's jury duty aside
segments.summary: Chuck mentions that his wife Emily was called for jury duty and was excused.

segments.title: Long-range weather forecasts and claimed accuracy
segments.summary: The almanacs sell millions of copies a year and claim an 80 percent accuracy for long-range weather forecasts. Their secret formula stories are discussed, and the Farmer's Almanac's pseudonymous forecaster Caleb Weatherby is mentioned. Both almanacs now use modern methods including sunspot activity.

segments.title: Climate normals and how forecasts are made
segments.summary: The almanacs use 30-year climate normals for temperature and precipitation by region and season, and call a forecast correct if it is slightly above or below average. Meteorologists are critical of this approach.

segments.title: Independent accuracy studies and why people still read them
segments.summary: Jan Null of Golden Gate Weather Service found the almanac was about 40 percent correct on precipitation and 6 percent on temperature for winter 2021-2022. A University of Illinois study found about 50 percent. The hosts discuss confirmation bias and the appeal of nature-focused folk traditions.

segments.title: Listener mail: Noam Chomsky is alive
segments.summary: A listener named Sam writes to confirm Noam Chomsky is still alive and recommends his political books.
